lesson.title: Metrics logs traces and useful telemetry
lesson.why: Collecting everything can still leave an incident unexplained. Useful telemetry connects user symptoms to a small set of testable operational hypotheses.
lesson.what: Choose metrics, logs, and traces by the questions they answer, then correlate them without exposing sensitive data.

concepts.name: Metrics summarize
concepts.body: Metrics aggregate numerical observations over time and dimensions. Counters track cumulative events; gauges represent current values; histograms describe distributions. They efficiently reveal rates and trends but usually cannot reconstruct the full story of one specific request.

concepts.name: Logs describe events
concepts.body: Structured logs capture discrete events with stable fields, severity, and timestamps. Include operation and correlation identifiers while excluding secrets and unnecessary personal data. Free-form messages alone make aggregation brittle and encourage expensive searches during urgent diagnosis.

concepts.name: Traces connect work
concepts.body: Traces link spans across a request path, exposing parent relationships and timing. They help identify where latency accumulates but sampling means not every request is retained. Propagation gaps can split one operation into apparently unrelated traces.

concepts.name: Operational questions
concepts.body: Start with user-visible success, latency, demand, and saturation. Then select diagnostic signals that distinguish plausible causes. Instrumentation has CPU, storage, and privacy costs; deleting low-value fields often improves both affordability and investigative clarity.

e2e: A request emits bounded measurements and structured operation events.
Context propagation links relevant spans and logs across service boundaries.
Aggregated metrics reveal an error or latency change.
Correlated trace and log evidence tests a specific cause before mitigation.

tasks.name: Calculate a user signal
steps: During one window, 1200 eligible requests include eighteen failures. Error ratio is 18/1200=1.5 percent and success is 98.5 percent. Exclude neither failures nor slow requests from the denominator merely because they are inconvenient, and define eligibility before interpreting the result.

tasks.name: Choose signal types
steps: Use a counter for request failures, a histogram for duration, a structured log for a rejected order reason, and a trace for cross-service delay. Explain why logging every successful request body is unnecessary for any of those four questions.

tasks.name: Design correlation fields
steps: Choose service name, environment, operation, trace ID, and safe error code for a fictional checkout event. Keep trace IDs in logs or traces rather than unbounded metric labels. Explain how that choice preserves per-request investigation without multiplying time series.

tasks.name: Diagnose missing evidence
steps: A dashboard shows normal latency while users report timeouts. Check whether failed requests emit duration, whether sampling drops slow spans, and whether the dashboard filters a region. Write one falsifiable hypothesis and identify the smallest additional signal needed to test it.

key_terms: Span: timed unit within a trace.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic request counts; do not collect production payloads or credentials for examples.
cleanup: Discard the telemetry field list; no collector or logging configuration changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, metrics show a latency spike but logs appear normal. How would you use traces without collecting every payload?
interview_points: Check metric coverage and trace sampling first.
Correlate operation and trace identifiers.
Inspect critical-path spans with bounded safe attributes.

storyboard.title: A metric symptom becomes a traceable hypothesis
storyboard.objective: Connect aggregate signals with request evidence.

scenes.title: Detect the symptom
scenes.caption: Aggregates reveal a change.
scenes.narration: The error ratio rises for a specific operation and time window.

scenes.title: Locate the failed span
scenes.caption: Trace context narrows the search.
scenes.narration: A sampled failed trace identifies the dependency where work stopped.

scenes.title: Test the cause
scenes.caption: A safe error code supplies context.
scenes.narration: The correlated structured event explains the rejection without exposing the request body.

observability/metrics-logs-traces-and-us.core: Metrics detect aggregate symptoms, traces locate request-path delays, and structured logs explain events. Design around questions, bounded dimensions, correlation, and privacy.

lesson.title: Prometheus scraping labels cardinality and PromQL
lesson.why: A useful metric can become an operational burden when labels create millions of series. Query semantics also determine whether dashboards tell the truth.
lesson.what: Connect scraping, time series, rate calculations, and histogram aggregation using small offline examples.

concepts.name: Scrape model
concepts.body: Prometheus periodically retrieves exposed metrics from targets. Target discovery and scrape health are distinct from application health: up indicates scrape success, not successful user transactions. Missing samples can result from target failure, network problems, or scrape configuration changes.

concepts.name: Label dimensions
concepts.body: Each unique label combination defines a separate time series. Bounded labels such as method or status class are manageable; user IDs and raw URLs often are not. Cardinality multiplies across dimensions and also affects ingestion, memory, queries, and retention cost.

concepts.name: Counter rates
concepts.body: Counters increase until reset. rate estimates per-second increase over a range and handles counter resets; summing rates across instances is generally preferable to taking a rate after aggregation because instance resets otherwise become harder to interpret correctly.

concepts.name: Distribution queries
concepts.body: Classic histogram buckets expose cumulative counts labeled by upper bound. Quantile estimation requires appropriate bucket aggregation and retaining the le dimension. Averaging precomputed per-instance percentiles is not a valid global percentile calculation; choose buckets matching the latency decisions you need.

e2e: Targets expose metrics with bounded names and labels.
Prometheus discovers targets and scrapes timestamped samples.
PromQL converts counters into rates and aggregates compatible dimensions.
Dashboards compare user signals with scrape health and missing-data evidence.

tasks.name: Calculate series growth
steps: A metric has four methods, six status classes, and twenty routes: 4*6*20=480 possible series per instance. Adding 10000 user IDs raises the potential to 4800000 per instance. Sparse combinations may reduce reality, but the extra dimension remains a serious design risk.

tasks.name: Compute a counter rate
steps: A synthetic counter rises from 1000 to 1600 over sixty seconds with no resets or gaps. Average rate is 600/60=10 requests per second. Explain why plotting 1600 as current throughput is incorrect and why real PromQL rate accounts for more than two ideal samples.

tasks.name: Review a query
steps: Interpret sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) as per-service request throughput. Keep a separate error numerator using the same eligibility and window. Explain why an absent target should not automatically appear as zero healthy traffic in a service-level availability calculation.

tasks.name: Diagnose misleading percentiles
steps: One instance serves ten requests with p95=20ms; another serves a thousand with p95=500ms. Their arithmetic mean of 260ms is not the fleet p95. Request mergeable histogram data and sufficient bucket resolution instead of inventing a weighted percentile formula.

key_terms: Series: metric name plus unique label set.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic metrics; do not expose a metrics endpoint publicly or generate high-cardinality load.
cleanup: Discard the query notes; no metrics storage was created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, Prometheus memory grows rapidly after adding a user label. How would you prove and correct the cause?
interview_points: Measure series growth by label and metric.
Remove unbounded dimensions and use logs for request identity.
Check retention, ingestion, and query impact after correction.

storyboard.title: One label can multiply every existing series
storyboard.objective: Explain cardinality growth at scrape ingestion.

scenes.title: Collect bounded dimensions
scenes.caption: Routes use normalized names.
scenes.narration: A small method and route label set produces predictable series counts.

scenes.title: Add user identifiers
scenes.caption: Unique combinations multiply.
scenes.narration: An unbounded user label expands ingestion and storage far beyond the original design.

scenes.title: Restore bounded labels
scenes.caption: Put request identity in another signal.
scenes.narration: Removing the user dimension controls new series while logs retain appropriate investigation context.

observability/prometheus-scraping-labels.core: Keep labels bounded, distinguish scrape success from user health, aggregate counter rates correctly, and compute fleet latency from mergeable distributions rather than averaged percentiles.

lesson.title: Grafana dashboards alerts and operational context
lesson.why: A polished dashboard can conceal missing data or unsupported conclusions. Operational views should guide decisions and provide the context needed during an incident.
lesson.what: Design a service dashboard and alert rule with explicit units, aggregation, no-data handling, and drill-down links.

concepts.name: Question-first panels
concepts.body: Each panel should answer an operational question, such as whether checkout errors increased or a dependency saturated. Show units, time range, aggregation, and meaningful legends. Avoid decorative gauges whose thresholds have no connection to user impact or capacity decisions.

concepts.name: Consistent comparisons
concepts.body: Compare signals over compatible windows and populations. Dashboard variables can silently filter away affected regions or versions. Annotate deployments and incidents so temporal correlations become visible, while remembering that simultaneous changes do not establish causation.

concepts.name: Alert evaluation
concepts.body: Alert rules evaluate queries and conditions independently of a person viewing a dashboard. Evaluation interval, pending period, and no-data or error behavior affect detection. A panel rendering successfully does not prove its alert rule is evaluated correctly.

concepts.name: Operational context
concepts.body: An alert should identify service, environment, severity, owner, and the next useful investigation step. Link to a focused dashboard and runbook with matching filters. Keep sensitive details out of notification labels and avoid routing every minor anomaly to paging.

e2e: A service owner defines user-facing health and diagnostic questions.
Panels visualize correctly aggregated signals with units and deployment context.
Alert evaluation detects sustained actionable conditions with explicit missing-data policy.
A routed notification opens matching investigation context and supports a bounded response.

tasks.name: Calculate pending behavior
steps: A rule evaluates every minute and requires a condition to remain true for five minutes. If first observed true at 10:00 and still true at 10:05, it can fire around 10:05, subject to evaluation behavior. A false result at 10:03 resets the pending continuity in this model.

tasks.name: Repair a misleading panel
steps: A panel titled latency displays an average of instance p95 values without units. Replace it with a correctly aggregated histogram quantile or clearly labeled per-instance series. Add milliseconds and the evaluation window, and explain why renaming the title alone does not fix the mathematics.

tasks.name: Design no-data handling
steps: A checkout metric disappears after an exporter crash. Decide how the rule treats no data and add scrape-health context. Compare an intentional quiet service with missing telemetry; setting both to healthy can hide outages while paging on every idle series can create noise.

tasks.name: Build a useful notification
steps: Write a synthetic alert containing checkout, staging, sustained error ratio, owner, and a dashboard link preserving time and environment. Include one safe diagnostic step and an escalation condition. Omit customer identifiers and avoid claiming the chart alone proves which dependency caused the incident.

key_terms: Pending period: sustained-condition delay before firing.
No data: missing query evidence, not automatic health.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic panels and rules; do not change live alert routing or suppress existing notifications.
cleanup: Discard the dashboard sketch; no Grafana resources were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a dashboard looks healthy while users report errors. Which visualization and alert assumptions would you verify?
interview_points: Check filters, windows, units, and population coverage.
Inspect missing-data behavior and independent alert evaluation.
Use deployment context as a hypothesis, not proof of causation.

storyboard.title: Missing telemetry must not look like healthy service
storyboard.objective: Connect panel interpretation and alert state.

scenes.title: Show service health
scenes.caption: The query covers the intended population.
scenes.narration: The dashboard and alert use explicit windows and service filters.

scenes.title: Exporter disappears
scenes.caption: No samples are not zero errors.
scenes.narration: Missing telemetry leaves insufficient evidence to call the service healthy.

scenes.title: Surface missing evidence
scenes.caption: Route an actionable telemetry condition.
scenes.narration: Explicit no-data handling points responders to scrape health and the matching dashboard.

observability/grafana-dashboards-alerts-.core: Dashboards need units, correct aggregation, population coverage, and context. Alerts evaluate independently and require explicit no-data behavior plus actionable ownership and links.
objectives: Explain alert pending and missing-data states

lesson.title: OpenTelemetry instrumentation propagation and collectors
lesson.why: Instrumentation that stops at service boundaries produces fragmented evidence. A reliable telemetry pipeline needs context continuity and controlled handling of data before export.
lesson.what: Trace spans and resource attributes through instrumentation, propagation, and Collector receivers, processors, and exporters.

concepts.name: Instrumentation boundary
concepts.body: Automatic instrumentation covers supported libraries quickly, while manual spans capture domain operations missing from generic network traces. Avoid duplicate spans from overlapping agents. Name operations consistently and use bounded attributes rather than embedding user data in span names.

concepts.name: Context propagation
concepts.body: Trace context crosses process boundaries through supported carriers such as HTTP headers. Inject on outgoing requests and extract on incoming work. Async jobs need deliberate parent or link semantics; simply copying a trace ID into a log does not establish proper span relationships.

concepts.name: Collector pipeline
concepts.body: The Collector receives, processes, and exports telemetry through configured pipelines. Components must be declared and referenced by the relevant service pipeline. Processors can batch, limit memory, and redact data, but ordering matters and unsupported transformations should not be assumed automatic.

concepts.name: Resource identity
concepts.body: Resource attributes identify the emitting service and deployment context. Distinguish them from per-operation attributes. Consistent service names improve cross-signal navigation; high-cardinality instance identifiers may be useful selectively but should not be copied indiscriminately into every metric dimension.

e2e: Instrumentation creates an operation span with safe bounded attributes.
Outgoing context is injected and extracted by the downstream service.
Telemetry reaches a Collector pipeline for limits, processing, and batching.
Exporters send approved data to backends while internal pipeline health is monitored.

tasks.name: Calculate span relationships
steps: A frontend root span calls API and cache; API calls database. There are four spans total, three parent-child edges, and one trace when context propagates correctly. If API starts a new trace instead, the database subtree separates and end-to-end causality becomes harder to inspect.

tasks.name: Place manual instrumentation
steps: A framework already traces incoming HTTP and database calls. Add one manual span for pricing-rule evaluation rather than wrapping every library call again. Choose rule-set version and safe outcome attributes, and explain why customer email should not become a span name or metric label.

tasks.name: Review a Collector path
steps: Draw OTLP receiver, memory limiter, attribute redaction, batch processor, and exporter. Verify each belongs to the trace pipeline and specify redaction before external export. Explain why declaring a processor block without referencing it does not make the pipeline use it.

tasks.name: Diagnose broken propagation
steps: Frontend and API traces appear separately after a proxy upgrade. Inspect header forwarding and server extraction before blaming backend storage. Test with synthetic requests, retain no authorization headers, and compare trace and parent IDs at the boundary to verify the fix.

key_terms: Resource attribute: identity of the telemetry producer.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic trace identifiers; never export real request headers or credentials during practice.
cleanup: Discard the span tree and pipeline diagram; no collectors were started.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, traces split at one service after a proxy change. How would you distinguish propagation failure from export failure?
interview_points: Compare incoming headers and extracted parent context safely.
Check whether spans exist but have different trace identities.
Inspect Collector and exporter health only after locating the boundary.

storyboard.title: Context joins service spans into one trace

scenes.title: Propagate parent context
scenes.caption: One request crosses a service boundary.
scenes.narration: The frontend injects context that the API extracts for its child span.

scenes.title: Proxy drops context
scenes.caption: The API starts an unrelated trace.
scenes.narration: Missing propagation headers split otherwise valid spans into separate traces.

scenes.title: Restore the carrier
scenes.caption: Verify parent identity before export.
scenes.narration: Correct forwarding and extraction restore the relationship before Collector processing.

observability/opentelemetry-instrumentat.core: Instrument domain work, propagate context explicitly, and connect Collector components in real pipelines. Use stable resource identity and redact sensitive attributes before export.

lesson.title: Centralized logging parsing retention and privacy
lesson.why: Centralized logs are powerful incident evidence and a concentrated data risk. Parsing and retention choices determine whether that evidence remains useful and appropriately protected.
lesson.what: Design structured event ingestion, bounded parsing, access controls, and retention using fictional log volume.

concepts.name: Structured events
concepts.body: Use stable field names, timestamps, severity, operation, and safe outcome codes. Preserve an original event identifier for deduplication where appropriate. Multi-line stack traces need explicit framing so collectors do not split one failure into unrelated records.

concepts.name: Parsing contracts
concepts.body: Parsers transform raw events into queryable fields. Format changes can silently drop fields or misclassify severity. Monitor parse errors and route malformed samples to a bounded diagnostic path rather than discarding all failures or indexing arbitrary unvalidated fields.

concepts.name: Retention tiers
concepts.body: Retention balances investigative needs, regulatory obligations, cost, and privacy. Hot searchable storage and archived data have different retrieval properties. Expiration and deletion procedures must include replicas, backups, and exports where applicable rather than assuming one index deletion erases every copy.

concepts.name: Privacy controls
concepts.body: Avoid collecting secrets and unnecessary personal data at the source; redact again before export as defense in depth. Restrict query and export permissions, audit access, and separate tenants. Hashing a low-entropy identifier does not automatically make the data anonymous.

e2e: Applications emit structured bounded events without sensitive payloads.
Collectors frame, parse, and validate records while tracking failures.
Approved fields reach access-controlled storage with defined retention.
Investigators query scoped evidence and expired data follows documented deletion policy.

tasks.name: Calculate retention volume
steps: A service emits 200 events per second averaging 500 bytes. Daily raw volume is 200*500*86400=8640000000 bytes, or 8.64 decimal GB. Seven days is 60.48 GB before indexing, replication, compression, and overhead; do not present raw volume as a vendor bill.

tasks.name: Design a log record
tasks.goal: Keep useful fields without payload leakage.
steps: Choose timestamp, service, operation, status, duration_ms, and synthetic trace_id for a checkout event. Exclude card data, authorization headers, and full request bodies. Explain how a safe error code can still distinguish validation failure from downstream timeout.

tasks.name: Diagnose parser regression
steps: A release renames severity to level but the parser still expects severity. Predict missing alert matches despite continued ingestion. Add schema-version handling and a parse-failure counter, then test representative old and new records before changing the production parser.

tasks.name: Review deletion scope
steps: A team promises thirty-day deletion but exports incident logs to indefinite object storage. Inventory searchable copies, exports, backups, and access paths. Define approved retention exceptions and deletion evidence rather than claiming that removing the primary index alone satisfies the promise.

key_terms: Parser: converting raw events into fields.
Redaction: removing protected information before exposure.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic events and counts; never copy real customer logs into exercises or public tools.
cleanup: Discard the sample schema and calculations; no log files were collected.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, logs still ingest after a release but error alerts stop firing. Which parsing and data-quality signals would you inspect?
interview_points: Compare schema fields and parser expectations across versions.
Check parse-error counters and missing-field rates.
Restore compatible parsing without exporting sensitive raw payloads.

storyboard.title: Ingestion success can hide parsing failure
storyboard.objective: Preserve queryable fields through schema changes.

scenes.title: Parse known fields
scenes.caption: Severity drives queries.
scenes.narration: The parser extracts expected fields from the known event schema.

scenes.title: Field name changes
scenes.caption: Bytes arrive but meaning is lost.
scenes.narration: A renamed severity field prevents existing error queries from matching.

scenes.title: Restore the parsing contract
scenes.caption: Monitor malformed and missing fields.
scenes.narration: Version-aware parsing and failure counters restore reliable queries without exposing raw secrets.

observability/centralized-logging-parsin.core: Centralized logging needs stable schemas, parse-failure monitoring, safe fields, scoped access, and retention covering every copy. Estimate raw volume separately from storage overhead and pricing.

lesson.title: Distributed tracing sampling and latency analysis
lesson.why: A slow trace does not mean every long span contributes equally to user latency. Sampling and concurrency shape what conclusions the evidence supports.
lesson.what: Analyze critical paths, head and tail sampling, missing spans, and clock assumptions using a small request timeline.

concepts.name: Critical path
concepts.body: End-to-end latency follows dependent work, not the sum of every span duration. Parallel child operations overlap. Separate exclusive execution time, waiting, and downstream duration so a large total of child spans does not create an impossible latency explanation.

concepts.name: Head sampling
concepts.body: Head sampling decides early whether to retain a trace, often probabilistically. It is efficient and bounded but cannot know the final outcome at request start. Rare errors may be underrepresented unless additional error signals or coordinated policies preserve visibility.

concepts.name: Tail sampling
concepts.body: Tail sampling buffers spans and decides after observing more of the trace, enabling selection by latency or errors. It needs memory, decision timing, and trace-aware routing. Late spans or traces split across collectors can undermine the intended policy.

concepts.name: Interpretation limits
concepts.body: Missing spans can reflect sampling, dropped exports, absent instrumentation, or propagation failure. Clock skew across hosts complicates absolute timeline comparisons. Use parent relationships and measured durations carefully, and corroborate a suspected bottleneck with metrics or profiling before changing capacity.

e2e: A request creates linked spans for synchronous and concurrent work.
Sampling policies choose which evidence to retain within capacity limits.
The backend assembles available spans into a trace timeline.
Investigators analyze the critical path and verify gaps before attributing latency.

tasks.name: Calculate critical-path latency
steps: A request spends 20ms before launching parallel calls A=80ms and B=120ms, waits for both, then spends 10ms responding. Ideal latency is 20+max(80,120)+10=150ms, not 230ms. Reducing A to 40ms does not change this critical path while B remains 120ms.

tasks.name: Estimate sampled evidence
steps: At 1 percent independent head sampling, 10000 requests yield about one hundred retained traces on average, not exactly one hundred. If only ten requests fail, expected retained failures are 0.1. Explain why absence of sampled error traces is weak evidence of no failures.

tasks.name: Review tail-sampling capacity
steps: Assume 500 traces per second and a ten-second decision window. Roughly 5000 in-flight traces may need buffering before overhead and bursts. Identify memory limits, late-span handling, and trace-affine routing as requirements before enabling a retain-all-errors policy.

tasks.name: Diagnose a timeline gap
tasks.goal: Separate missing evidence from idle time.
steps: An API span lasts 600ms but visible children account for only 100ms. Consider queue wait, uninstrumented work, export loss, and runtime pauses. Add one targeted span or profile in a disposable test rather than declaring the unexplained 500ms to be network latency automatically.

key_terms: Critical path: longest dependent work chain.
Tail sampling: decision after buffering trace evidence.
Exclusive time: span time excluding child work.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic timings; do not capture production payloads or enable unbounded tracing.
cleanup: Discard the timeline; no trace backend or collector settings changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, optimizing a long child span does not improve request latency. What trace relationships might explain the result?
interview_points: Check parallelism and the true critical path.
Inspect waiting and uninstrumented exclusive work.
Validate sampling completeness before drawing broad conclusions.

storyboard.title: Parallel spans do not add directly to response time
storyboard.objective: Identify the branch that limits completion.

scenes.title: Start both calls
scenes.caption: The parent waits for both results.
scenes.narration: Parallel child durations overlap instead of adding sequentially.

scenes.title: A finishes first
scenes.caption: B still determines the wait.
scenes.narration: The parent cannot complete while the slower required branch remains active.

scenes.title: Target the limiting branch
scenes.caption: Optimize the critical path.
scenes.narration: Reducing B can shorten the response, while making already-faster A faster may not.

observability/distributed-tracing-sampli.core: Analyze dependent critical paths rather than summing spans. Sampling changes evidence coverage; tail policies require bounded buffers and trace-aware routing. Missing spans do not identify a cause by themselves.

lesson.title: Alert design routing deduplication and on-call noise
lesson.why: Too many low-value pages delay response to real incidents. Alerting should summon the right person for actionable user impact, not merely announce every changing metric.
lesson.what: Design symptom-based alerts with grouping, inhibition, ownership, and measurable response quality.

concepts.name: Actionable symptoms
concepts.body: Page when a condition needs prompt human action to protect users or a defined reliability objective. Diagnostic anomalies can remain dashboards or tickets. Include clear urgency and a safe first step; a notification with no possible action is usually not a useful page.

concepts.name: Grouping and deduplication
concepts.body: Group related alerts into incident-level notifications using stable labels. Deduplication avoids repeatedly notifying the same continuing condition. Overly broad grouping can hide separate failures, while volatile labels such as timestamps defeat deduplication and create notification storms.

concepts.name: Routing and inhibition
concepts.body: Route by service ownership and severity, with explicit fallback when ownership is missing. Inhibition suppresses downstream symptom notifications while a known parent condition is firing. It should reduce noise without suppressing unrelated impact or permanently hiding recovery failures.

concepts.name: Quality measurement
concepts.body: Track actionable page rate, time to acknowledge, duplicate volume, and missed incidents. Review alerts after incidents and during routine operations. Silence and maintenance windows need scope and expiry; indefinite broad silences can turn quiet dashboards into undetected outages.

e2e: A sustained user-impact signal enters an alerting rule.
Stable labels group and deduplicate related firing instances.
Routing chooses an owner while narrow inhibition reduces dependent noise.
The responder acts, verifies recovery, and feeds alert quality observations into review.

tasks.name: Calculate noise reduction
steps: Forty Pods fail behind one unavailable database and each emits three notifications: 120 notifications. Grouping by service and incident condition could produce one initial grouped notification plus planned updates. Do not claim all forty failures are harmless; preserve their detail inside the incident context.

tasks.name: Choose a paging condition
steps: Compare high CPU with sustained checkout failure. Page on actionable checkout impact and include CPU as diagnostic context unless CPU itself predicts an urgent defined failure. Explain why a busy but healthy batch worker should not page the customer-facing on-call team automatically.

tasks.name: Review inhibition scope
steps: A database outage inhibits connection-failure alerts for its dependent API. A separate authentication outage should still notify its owner. Define dependency labels precisely and test this counterexample instead of suppressing every alert sharing the same region.

tasks.name: Audit a silence
steps: A planned maintenance silence covers one service for thirty minutes with an owner and ticket reference. Contrast it with an indefinite all-services silence. Define expiry verification and a post-maintenance synthetic check so a quiet notification channel is not mistaken for restored health.

key_terms: Inhibition: conditional suppression of related alerts.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic alerts; do not silence live pages, modify on-call schedules, or send notifications.
cleanup: Discard the routing matrix; existing alert policies remain unchanged.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, one dependency outage generates hundreds of pages. How would you reduce noise without hiding independent failures?
interview_points: Group stable service and incident labels.
Use precise dependency-based inhibition with counterexample tests.
Keep ownership, expiry, and impact detail visible.

storyboard.title: One outage should not become hundreds of unrelated pages
storyboard.objective: Group dependent symptoms while preserving separate incidents.

scenes.title: Dependency fails
scenes.caption: Many instances share one symptom.
scenes.narration: The database outage produces connection failures across API replicas.

scenes.title: Duplicate pages multiply
scenes.caption: Instance-level notifications obscure context.
scenes.narration: Repeated alerts overwhelm the responder without adding a new required action.

scenes.title: Group and route
scenes.caption: Keep details inside one actionable incident.
scenes.narration: Stable grouping and narrow inhibition produce a useful notification with ownership and dependent evidence.

observability/alert-design-routing-dedup.core: Page for actionable impact, group with stable labels, route by ownership, and inhibit only proven dependent noise. Audit silences and measure page quality, not just notification count.

lesson.title: Synthetic monitoring real-user monitoring and profiling
lesson.why: No single observation captures both user experience and internal execution cost. Synthetic tests, real-user measurements, and profiles answer complementary questions.
lesson.what: Compare controlled journey checks, actual browser experience, and code-level resource profiles without collecting personal browsing data.

concepts.name: Synthetic journeys
concepts.body: Synthetic monitoring runs controlled probes or scripted transactions from known locations. It detects availability even when traffic is low and provides repeatable checks. Its accounts, network paths, and data may differ from real users, so passing probes do not prove universal health.

concepts.name: Real-user measurements
concepts.body: RUM observes actual client experiences, including device, network, and rendering effects. Aggregate by bounded useful dimensions and apply consent, minimization, and privacy rules. Sampling and browser support bias the observed population; missing clients must not be treated as satisfied users.

concepts.name: Runtime profiling
concepts.body: Profiles sample where CPU, allocation, lock contention, or wall time is spent. CPU profiles do not directly explain time waiting on remote services. Profiling overhead and symbol quality matter; interpret stacks with workload context rather than optimizing the tallest bar blindly.

concepts.name: Triangulation
concepts.body: Combine user outcomes, controlled probes, traces, and profiles to distinguish client rendering, network delay, backend latency, and expensive code paths. Correlation narrows hypotheses but needs a measured change or targeted experiment before claiming a causal performance improvement.

e2e: Synthetic journeys continuously test a defined service path.
Privacy-aware RUM summarizes actual client outcomes across relevant cohorts.
A discrepancy identifies where traces or profiling should investigate further.
A bounded change is evaluated against both user experience and resource behavior.

tasks.name: Calculate probe availability
steps: A synthetic check runs every minute for one hour and fails three times: 57/60=95 percent successful checks. This is probe success, not necessarily 95 percent of real users succeeding. Record probe location and transaction coverage before comparing it with an application SLO.

tasks.name: Compare user cohorts
steps: Desktop clients show two-second page loads while low-end mobile clients show eight seconds. A datacenter synthetic probe reports one second. Explain why network, device CPU, and rendering can produce all three results without a contradiction, and choose bounded device-class dimensions for investigation.

tasks.name: Choose the right profile
steps: An endpoint takes two seconds but uses only 100ms of CPU. A CPU profile cannot account for the full wait. Inspect wall-time traces, blocking, and downstream calls first; use CPU profiling when evidence indicates execution cost rather than simply increasing sampling frequency.

tasks.name: Plan a safe improvement test
steps: A profile suggests repeated JSON parsing. Propose caching parsed immutable configuration in a disposable benchmark, compare CPU and latency, then consider memory and invalidation costs. Require representative client experience checks before claiming the optimization fixes all users' slow pages.

key_terms: RUM: measurements from real client sessions.
Cohort: bounded group for meaningful comparison.
lesson.safety: Use fictional measurements; do not record real browsing sessions, credentials, or personal device identifiers.
cleanup: Discard the cohort and timing tables; no monitoring probes were deployed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, synthetic tests pass while mobile users report slow pages. How would you narrow the cause without assuming backend failure?
interview_points: Compare client cohorts, locations, and probe coverage.
Separate rendering, network, backend, and CPU evidence.
Validate a targeted change across representative user populations.

storyboard.title: Controlled probes and real clients see different paths
storyboard.objective: Combine external experience with code-level evidence.

scenes.title: Probe succeeds
scenes.caption: One controlled path is healthy.
scenes.narration: The synthetic journey completes quickly from its configured environment.

scenes.title: Mobile remains slow

observability/synthetic-monitoring-real-.core: Synthetic checks provide repeatability, RUM shows actual client diversity, and profiling reveals resource execution. Interpret coverage and privacy limits, then test a specific performance hypothesis.

lesson.title: Telemetry pipelines capacity security and cost
lesson.why: Telemetry often fails during the incident when it is most needed. Capacity, backpressure, security, and retention must be designed as an operational system.
lesson.what: Size a bounded collection pipeline and choose explicit behavior when ingestion or export cannot keep up.

concepts.name: Flow and buffering
concepts.body: Receivers ingest data, processors transform it, and exporters send it onward. Queues absorb temporary mismatch but do not create throughput. A sustained input rate above output capacity eventually fills every finite buffer unless data is dropped or producers slow down.

concepts.name: Failure containment
concepts.body: Memory limits, retry budgets, bounded queues, and disk persistence can protect collectors during downstream outages. Persistent queues improve durability only within their configured limits and failure model. Monitor refused, dropped, queued, and exported data independently rather than relying on process uptime.

concepts.name: Security boundaries
concepts.body: Authenticate producers where supported, protect transport, restrict endpoints, and minimize sensitive attributes before crossing trust boundaries. Multi-tenant pipelines need authorization and isolation, not just tenant labels supplied by clients. A caller-controlled tenant field is not proof of tenant identity.

concepts.name: Economic controls
concepts.body: Cardinality, sampling, event size, retention, and replication drive volume. Use service-level budgets and high-value signals before indiscriminate sampling. Cost reductions should be tested against incident and compliance needs; removing all error evidence can make a cheap pipeline operationally useless.

e2e: Authenticated producers emit bounded telemetry into configured receivers.
Processors enforce limits, remove protected data, and batch accepted records.
Queues and retries absorb short export failures within explicit budgets.
Internal pipeline metrics reveal saturation or loss and trigger a controlled response.

tasks.name: Calculate buffer exhaustion
steps: Input is 12000 events per second and export capacity is 10000. Backlog grows by 2000 per second. A queue holding 600000 events fills in 300 seconds from empty, or five minutes, before overhead and bursts. Adding queue space delays failure but does not solve the rate mismatch.

tasks.name: Choose loss policy
steps: During an exporter outage, prioritize security-relevant records and representative error traces while bounding routine debug events. Explain which records may be dropped, where counters record loss, and why retries without a limit can consume all memory during a prolonged outage.

tasks.name: Review tenant trust
steps: A public receiver trusts an incoming tenant_id attribute. An attacker can claim another tenant. Bind tenant routing to authenticated identity or an authorized gateway mapping, and reject arbitrary overrides. Keep access checks independent from dashboard filters and descriptive labels.

tasks.name: Estimate raw daily traffic
steps: At 10000 events per second and 300 bytes each, raw daily traffic is 259200000000 bytes, or 259.2 decimal GB. Model compression, indexing, replication, and retention separately. Use contractual unit rates only when available; do not invent current service prices from this volume.

key_terms: Backpressure: slowing producers when downstream is saturated.
Export retry: repeated delivery attempt after failure.
Pipeline loss: telemetry rejected or dropped before retention.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic rates; do not flood collectors, open public receivers, or change live retention.
cleanup: Discard the capacity worksheet; no pipeline components were started.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, collectors remain running but incident traces disappear during backend outages. Which internal signals and limits would you inspect?
interview_points: Check queue growth, export failures, refusals, and drops.
Compare sustained ingress with export capacity.
Review bounded persistence, retries, and evidence-priority policy.

observability/telemetry-pipelines-capaci.core: Size telemetry as a bounded flow system. Queues cannot fix sustained overload; monitor loss, authenticate tenant identity, minimize sensitive data, and model volume before cost.
